desc:
A number is self-describing when, for every position i counted from 0 at the left, the digit in that position equals the number of times the digit i occurs in the whole number. For example 2020 is self-describing: it has two 0s, two 2s, no 1s and no 3s, which matches the digits 2, 0, 2, 0 in positions 0 to 3.

Given the length d, return all self-describing numbers with exactly d digits, in increasing order.

d = 4 -> [1210, 2020]
d = 5 -> [21200]
d = 3 -> []
hints: Think of the number as a list c of d digits, where c[i] must equal the count of value i in the list. Every entry is at most d, and the entries must add up to d, since each digit is counted once.
So the candidates are sequences of d non-negative integers with sum d. Build them one entry at a time while tracking the remaining total, which keeps the search small.
Once a candidate is complete, count how often each value 0 to d-1 occurs and compare it with the candidate. There are only C(2d-1, d) candidates, which is 1716 for d = 7.
editorial: Let the digits be c<sub>0</sub>, ..., c<sub>d-1</sub>. The rule says c<sub>i</sub> is the number of positions j with c<sub>j</sub> = i. Each digit is counted exactly once across the values, so the digits sum to d. The candidates are therefore the weak compositions of d into d parts, of which there are C(2d-1, d).

For each candidate, count the occurrences of 0 to d-1 and compare them with the candidate. The first digit is automatically nonzero: a leading 0 would require c<sub>0</sub> = 0, meaning no digit is 0, which contradicts that digit itself being 0. So every match is a genuine d-digit number.

The search is generated in lexicographic order of the digits, which is numeric order for numbers of the same length, so no sorting is needed. For reference, the lengths with solutions up to 7 are 4 (1210, 2020), 5 (21200) and 7 (3211000).
